content.shloka:
Shraaddhena kalpitam pitroh anushtitam vidhaanatah |
Annena udakena cha vai triptim yaanti pitaamahah ||
content.meaning: By performing Shraddha for one's ancestors according to prescribed rites, offering food and water, the forefathers attain complete satisfaction and contentment.
content.transliteration:
Śrāddhena kalpitaṁ pitroḥ anuṣṭhitaṁ vidhānataḥ |
Annena udakena ca vai tṛptiṁ yānti pitāmahāḥ ||

content.shloka: Shraddha is a sacred Hindu ritual performed to pay homage to departed ancestors (Pitrs). It is an act of gratitude and devotion through which the living offer food, water, and prayers to ensure peace and liberation for the souls of their forebears.
content.meaning: The word 'Shraddha' comes from 'Shraddha' (faith). It signifies that the ritual must be performed with complete faith, devotion, and sincerity. Without true faith, the ritual is considered incomplete regardless of how elaborately it is performed.
content.transliteration: Shraddha is a sacred Hindu ritual performed to pay homage to departed ancestors (Pitrs). It is an act of gratitude and devotion through which the living offer food, water, and prayers to ensure peace and liberation for the souls of their forebears.

content.shloka: General Shraddha Procedure: 1) Perform Sankalpa (sacred vow) stating the names of ancestors. 2) Invite an odd number of Brahmins (1, 3, 5, etc.) to represent the Pitrs and Devatas. 3) Offer Arghya (water oblation) and perform Pind Daan (rice ball offering). 4) Feed the Brahmins a sattvic meal. 5) Offer Dakshina (monetary offering). 6) Feed crows, cows, and dogs with the Shraddha food.
content.meaning: The three rice balls (pindas) offered during Shraddha represent three generations of ancestors — father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The ritual creates a spiritual bridge between the living and the departed, allowing blessings to flow in both directions.
content.transliteration: General Shraddha Procedure: 1) Perform Sankalpa (sacred vow) stating the names of ancestors. 2) Invite an odd number of Brahmins (1, 3, 5, etc.) to represent the Pitrs and Devatas. 3) Offer Arghya (water oblation) and perform Pind Daan (rice ball offering). 4) Feed the Brahmins a sattvic meal. 5) Offer Dakshina (monetary offering). 6) Feed crows, cows, and dogs with the Shraddha food.

content.shloka:
Devataa bhyah pitribhyashcha mahaa yogibhya eva cha |
Namah svadhaa yai svaahaa yai nityam eva namo namah ||
content.meaning: To the Devatas, to the Pitrs (ancestors), and to the great Yogis — salutations! To Svadha (the sacred offering to ancestors) and Svaha (the sacred offering to gods), eternal salutations again and again.
content.transliteration:
Devatābhyaḥ pitṛbhyaśca mahāyogibhya eva ca |
Namaḥ svadhāyai svāhāyai nityam eva namo namaḥ ||

content.shloka: Important rules: Shraddha should be performed facing south (Pitrs reside in the southern direction). Use black sesame seeds (til) as they are sacred to Pitrs. The food should include rice, dal, vegetables, and kheer. Shraddha should never be performed after sunset.
content.meaning: The performer (Karta) should observe fasting or eat only once on the day of Shraddha. He should maintain purity of body and mind, avoid anger and harsh words, and perform the ritual with calm devotion. The merit of Shraddha is said to sustain the ancestors for an entire year.
content.transliteration: Important rules: Shraddha should be performed facing south (Pitrs reside in the southern direction). Use black sesame seeds (til) as they are sacred to Pitrs. The food should include rice, dal, vegetables, and kheer. Shraddha should never be performed after sunset.

content.shloka:
Pitru paksha ashvina maase krishna pakshe vishesha tah |
Shraaddham kurvanti ye martyaah te yaanti paramaam gatim ||
content.meaning: Those mortals who perform Shraddha during the Pitru Paksha (the dark fortnight of the month of Ashvina) attain the supreme destination.
content.transliteration:
Pitṛ pakṣa āśvina māse kṛṣṇa pakṣe viśeṣataḥ |
Śrāddhaṁ kurvanti ye martyāḥ te yānti paramāṁ gatim ||

content.shloka: Pitru Paksha (also called Mahalaya Paksha) is a 16-day period in the Hindu month of Ashvina (September-October) dedicated exclusively to honoring ancestors. It begins on Purnima and ends on Amavasya (Sarva Pitru Amavasya).
content.meaning: During this period, the gates between the world of the living and the realm of the ancestors are believed to be open. Ancestors descend to the mortal plane to receive offerings from their descendants. Failing to perform Shraddha during this period is said to cause the ancestors great distress.
content.transliteration: Pitru Paksha (also called Mahalaya Paksha) is a 16-day period in the Hindu month of Ashvina (September-October) dedicated exclusively to honoring ancestors. It begins on Purnima and ends on Amavasya (Sarva Pitru Amavasya).

content.shloka: Each of the 16 days of Pitru Paksha corresponds to a specific tithi (lunar day). The Shraddha for each ancestor is performed on the tithi that matches their death anniversary. If the exact tithi is unknown, Sarva Pitru Amavasya (the last day) covers all ancestors.
content.meaning: Key dates: Chaturthi — for those who died young. Navami (Avidhava Navami) — for married women who passed before their husbands. Dwadashi — for Sannyasis (renunciants). Chaturdashi — for those who died in accidents or by unnatural causes. Amavasya — for all ancestors collectively.
content.transliteration: Each of the 16 days of Pitru Paksha corresponds to a specific tithi (lunar day). The Shraddha for each ancestor is performed on the tithi that matches their death anniversary. If the exact tithi is unknown, Sarva Pitru Amavasya (the last day) covers all ancestors.

content.shloka:
Pitroonaam akriyaanaam cha duhkhinaam yatra kutra vaa |
Sarva pitru amaavasya tithau shreshtham daanam bhavet ||
content.meaning: For those ancestors whose rites have not been performed, or who died in suffering anywhere, the offering made on Sarva Pitru Amavasya is the most excellent charity and brings them peace.
content.transliteration:
Pitṝṇām akṛiyāṇāṁ ca duḥkhināṁ yatra kutra vā |
Sarva pitṛ amāvasyā tithau śreṣṭhaṁ dānaṁ bhavet ||

content.shloka: During Pitru Paksha, devotees also visit sacred pilgrimage sites like Gaya, Varanasi, Prayag, and Rameshwaram to perform Pind Daan. The merit of Shraddha at Gaya is considered especially powerful.
content.meaning: In daily life during Pitru Paksha, one should avoid starting new ventures, purchasing new items, or celebrating joyous occasions. The focus should be entirely on reverence, remembrance, and service to ancestors through prescribed rituals.
content.transliteration: During Pitru Paksha, devotees also visit sacred pilgrimage sites like Gaya, Varanasi, Prayag, and Rameshwaram to perform Pind Daan. The merit of Shraddha at Gaya is considered especially powerful.

content.shloka:
Om pitrubhyah svadhaa namah | Om pitaamahebhyah svadhaa namah |
Om prapitaamahebhyah svadhaa namah ||
content.meaning: Om, to the fathers — svadha (offering) and salutations. Om, to the grandfathers — svadha and salutations. Om, to the great-grandfathers — svadha and salutations.
content.transliteration:
Om pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ | Om pitāmahebhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ |
Om prapitāmahebhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ ||

content.shloka: Pind Daan is the offering of rice balls (pindas) to the departed ancestors. The pindas are made from cooked rice mixed with black sesame seeds, barley flour, honey, and ghee. Three pindas are prepared for three generations of ancestors.
content.meaning: The word 'Pinda' literally means 'a ball or body.' The offering symbolizes providing a new spiritual body to the ancestors in the afterlife. Through this ritual, the departed souls receive nourishment and are aided in their journey towards liberation.
content.transliteration: Pind Daan is the offering of rice balls (pindas) to the departed ancestors. The pindas are made from cooked rice mixed with black sesame seeds, barley flour, honey, and ghee. Three pindas are prepared for three generations of ancestors.

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Sit facing south on a clean surface. 2) Spread darbha (kusha) grass. 3) Place three pindas on the grass while chanting the ancestor mantras. 4) Offer water (tarpan) around each pinda. 5) Sprinkle black sesame seeds. 6) Place the pindas in a river, under a peepal tree, or where crows can eat them.
content.meaning: If a crow eats the pinda, it is considered a sign that the ancestors have accepted the offering and are satisfied. If the crow does not eat, the ritual may be repeated with additional prayers.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Sit facing south on a clean surface. 2) Spread darbha (kusha) grass. 3) Place three pindas on the grass while chanting the ancestor mantras. 4) Offer water (tarpan) around each pinda. 5) Sprinkle black sesame seeds. 6) Place the pindas in a river, under a peepal tree, or where crows can eat them.

content.shloka:
Ye me kulaanukulashcha pitarah sva pitur yuge |
Teshaam sarvesham triptaye idam astu tilodakam ||
content.meaning: For all my ancestors across all generations in my family lineage — may this offering of sesame seeds and water bring them complete satisfaction.
content.transliteration:
Ye me kulānukulāśca pitaraḥ sva pitur yuge |
Teṣāṁ sarveṣāṁ tṛptaye idaṁ astu tilodakam ||

content.shloka:
Tarpayaami pitrin sarvaan udakena samanvitam |
Ye me pitarah ye me pitaamahah ye me pra-pitaamahah |
Taan sarvaan tarpayaami ||
content.meaning: I offer water oblation to all my ancestors — my father, my grandfather, and my great-grandfather and all who came before them. I satisfy them all with this water offering.
content.transliteration:
Tarpayāmi pitṝn sarvān udakena samanvitam |
Ye me pitaraḥ ye me pitāmahāḥ ye me prapitāmahāḥ |
Tān sarvān tarpayāmi ||

content.shloka: Tarpan (water oblation) is one of the simplest yet most powerful Shraddha rituals. It involves offering water mixed with black sesame seeds, barley, and kusha grass to the ancestors while chanting their names and gotras.
content.meaning: Tarpan can be performed daily during Pitru Paksha, on Amavasya days, on the death anniversary (Punyatithi), or on any day with devotion. It provides immediate relief and satisfaction to the departed souls.
content.transliteration: Tarpan (water oblation) is one of the simplest yet most powerful Shraddha rituals. It involves offering water mixed with black sesame seeds, barley, and kusha grass to the ancestors while chanting their names and gotras.

content.shloka: Tarpan Procedure: 1) Face south. 2) Wear the sacred thread (Yajnopavita) on the right shoulder (Prachinavarti/Apasavya). 3) Take water with black sesame in cupped hands. 4) Pour between the thumb and index finger (Pitru Tirtha) while chanting each ancestor's name and gotra. 5) Perform at least three tarpans for each ancestor.
content.meaning: The direction of pouring water is crucial: offerings to gods flow from the finger tips, to sages from the base of the little finger, and to ancestors from the space between the thumb and index finger. This distinction must be observed carefully.
content.transliteration: Tarpan Procedure: 1) Face south. 2) Wear the sacred thread (Yajnopavita) on the right shoulder (Prachinavarti/Apasavya). 3) Take water with black sesame in cupped hands. 4) Pour between the thumb and index finger (Pitru Tirtha) while chanting each ancestor's name and gotra. 5) Perform at least three tarpans for each ancestor.

content.shloka:
Om __[Name]__ gotraanaam __[Gotra]__ sharmanaam vasu roopinaam
Pitrin svadhaa namah tarpayaami ||
content.meaning: This is the standard tarpan formula where you insert the ancestor's name and gotra. 'Vasu rupinaam' for father, 'Rudra rupinaam' for grandfather, and 'Aditya rupinaam' for great-grandfather.
content.transliteration:
Om ___[Nāma]___ gotrāṇāṁ ___[Gotra]___ śarmaṇāṁ vasu rūpiṇāṁ
Pitṝn svadhā namaḥ tarpayāmi ||

content.shloka: After completing tarpan for paternal ancestors (father, grandfather, great-grandfather), the same should be performed for maternal ancestors (maternal grandfather, etc.). The sacred thread position changes back to normal (Savya) after the ritual.
content.meaning: Even those who do not know the names or gotras of all their ancestors can perform tarpan by using the general formula 'Ye ke chaasmat kule jaataah' (whoever was born in our lineage). This ensures all ancestors receive the offering.
content.transliteration: After completing tarpan for paternal ancestors (father, grandfather, great-grandfather), the same should be performed for maternal ancestors (maternal grandfather, etc.). The sacred thread position changes back to normal (Savya) after the ritual.

content.shloka:
Gayaam gatvaa kriyaam kritvaa pinda daanam samaacharana |
Trini vamshaani uddharet tasmaat gayaa tirtham vishishyate ||
content.meaning: Having gone to Gaya and performed the rites, offering Pind Daan according to tradition, one liberates three generations. Therefore, the holy site of Gaya is considered the most distinguished.
content.transliteration:
Gayāṁ gatvā kriyāṁ kṛtvā piṇḍa dānaṁ samācaraṇa |
Triṇi vaṁśāni uddharet tasmāt Gayā tīrthaṁ viśiṣyate ||

content.shloka: Gaya in Bihar is the most sacred place for performing Shraddha and Pind Daan in the entire Hindu world. It is believed that Lord Vishnu Himself resides on the Gaya Akshayavat (the immortal banyan tree) as Gadhadhara (wielder of the mace).
content.meaning: According to the Vayu Purana, performing Pind Daan at Gaya liberates not just three but seven generations of ancestors from the cycle of birth and death. Lord Rama Himself performed Shraddha for His father Dasharatha at Gaya.
content.transliteration: Gaya in Bihar is the most sacred place for performing Shraddha and Pind Daan in the entire Hindu world. It is believed that Lord Vishnu Himself resides on the Gaya Akshayavat (the immortal banyan tree) as Gadhadhara (wielder of the mace).

content.shloka: The main pilgrimage sites in Gaya for Pind Daan include: 1) Vishnupad Temple — the footprint of Lord Vishnu. 2) Falgu River — the sacred river for tarpan. 3) Akshayavat — the immortal banyan tree. 4) Pretshila Hill — the hill of departed souls. 5) Ramshila — where Lord Rama performed Shraddha.
content.meaning: The complete Gaya pilgrimage involves performing Pind Daan at multiple sacred spots (known as Vedis) over several days. A qualified Gaya-wal (priest specializing in Gaya rituals) guides the pilgrim through the elaborate ceremonies.
content.transliteration: The main pilgrimage sites in Gaya for Pind Daan include: 1) Vishnupad Temple — the footprint of Lord Vishnu. 2) Falgu River — the sacred river for tarpan. 3) Akshayavat — the immortal banyan tree. 4) Pretshila Hill — the hill of departed souls. 5) Ramshila — where Lord Rama performed Shraddha.

content.shloka:
Akshayam vat moolasthitam pind daanam mahaaphalam |
Yaavat pindah sthitah tatra taavat pita sukhee bhavet ||
content.meaning: The Pind Daan offered at the root of the Akshayavat (immortal banyan tree) yields imperishable fruit. As long as the pinda remains at that sacred spot, the ancestors continue to experience happiness.
content.transliteration:
Akṣayaṁ vaṭa mūlasthitaṁ piṇḍa dānaṁ mahāphalam |
Yāvat piṇḍaḥ sthitaḥ tatra tāvat pitā sukhī bhavet ||

content.shloka:
Mritasya yat dine karma kriyate tattu vai smritam |
Tithi shraaddham iti proktam sarva paapa pramoochanam ||
content.meaning: The ritual performed on the death anniversary (tithi) of the departed is called Tithi Shraddha. It is said to be the remover of all sins.
content.transliteration:
Mṛtasya yat dine karma kriyate tattu vai smṛtam |
Tithi śrāddhaṁ iti proktaṁ sarva pāpa pramocanaṁ ||

content.shloka: Tithi Shraddha is the annual Shraddha performed on the exact lunar tithi (date) when the ancestor passed away. It is the most important annual duty of a Hindu householder towards their departed parents and ancestors.
content.meaning: The tithi is calculated according to the Hindu lunar calendar, not the English calendar. The exact matching of the lunar month, paksha (fortnight), and tithi is essential for the ritual to reach the intended ancestor.
content.transliteration: Tithi Shraddha is the annual Shraddha performed on the exact lunar tithi (date) when the ancestor passed away. It is the most important annual duty of a Hindu householder towards their departed parents and ancestors.

content.shloka: Preparation: 1) Identify the correct tithi from the Hindu calendar. 2) Invite Brahmins a day in advance. 3) Prepare sattvic food — rice, dal, vegetables, kheer, puris, and seasonal fruits. 4) Arrange items for puja — flowers, incense, darbha grass, black sesame, barley, kusha grass, and sacred water.
content.meaning: The food prepared for Tithi Shraddha should not include onion, garlic, masoor dal, or any rajasic/tamasic items. The cooking should be done in silence with devotion, preferably using ghee and traditional recipes that the departed ancestor enjoyed.
content.transliteration: Preparation: 1) Identify the correct tithi from the Hindu calendar. 2) Invite Brahmins a day in advance. 3) Prepare sattvic food — rice, dal, vegetables, kheer, puris, and seasonal fruits. 4) Arrange items for puja — flowers, incense, darbha grass, black sesame, barley, kusha grass, and sacred water.

content.shloka:
Om agne kavyavaahana pitrin aavaha iha aagataah |
Te bhunktataam pravishataam tantu mahya hutam havih ||
content.meaning: O Agni, the bearer of offerings to the ancestors, bring the Pitrs here. Let them come, partake of the offerings, and enter the sacred thread of this ritual. May this oblation reach them.
content.transliteration:
Om Agne kavyavāhana pitṝn āvaha iha āgatāḥ |
Te bhuñktāṁ praviśatāṁ tantu mahya hutaṁ haviḥ ||

content.shloka: After feeding the Brahmins and performing all rituals, the Karta (performer) should eat the remaining prasad food along with family members. The merit of Tithi Shraddha sustains the ancestor for one full year until the next annual ceremony.
content.meaning: If the exact tithi cannot be observed due to unavoidable circumstances, it can be performed on the next day or during Pitru Paksha. However, every effort should be made to observe the correct tithi, as it has the maximum spiritual impact.
content.transliteration: After feeding the Brahmins and performing all rituals, the Karta (performer) should eat the remaining prasad food along with family members. The merit of Tithi Shraddha sustains the ancestor for one full year until the next annual ceremony.

content.shloka: Narayan Bali is an elaborate Vedic ritual performed to liberate the souls of ancestors who died an unnatural death — accident, suicide, murder, or from a curse. These souls are believed to become Preta (restless spirits) unable to find peace.
content.meaning: This ritual is also performed when a family faces repeated misfortunes, unexplained illnesses, or obstacles in marriage and progeny — which are often attributed to the suffering of unresolved ancestral souls (Pitru Dosha).
content.transliteration: Narayan Bali is an elaborate Vedic ritual performed to liberate the souls of ancestors who died an unnatural death — accident, suicide, murder, or from a curse. These souls are believed to become Preta (restless spirits) unable to find peace.

content.shloka:
Om Narayanam mahaajnanam devam shanka gadaa dharam |
Pretaan mochanam devesham namaste purushottamam ||
content.meaning: Om, salutations to Lord Narayana, the omniscient Supreme Lord who bears the conch and mace, the liberator of all restless spirits, the God of gods, Purushottam.
content.transliteration:
Om Nārāyaṇaṁ mahājñānaṁ devaṁ śaṅkha gadā dharaṁ |
Pretān mocanaṁ deveśaṁ namaste puruṣottamaṁ ||

content.shloka: The Narayan Bali involves: 1) Creating a symbolic effigy of the deceased from darbha grass. 2) Performing a complete set of funeral rites (Antyeshti Kriya) as if the person died naturally. 3) Offering Pind Daan and Tarpan. 4) Invoking Lord Narayana for the liberation of the soul. 5) Immersing the effigy in a sacred river.
content.meaning: This ritual must be performed by qualified Brahmin priests who are well-versed in the Atharva Veda and Garuda Purana. The ideal locations for Narayan Bali are Trimbakeshwar (Nashik), Gaya, and Varanasi.
content.transliteration: The Narayan Bali involves: 1) Creating a symbolic effigy of the deceased from darbha grass. 2) Performing a complete set of funeral rites (Antyeshti Kriya) as if the person died naturally. 3) Offering Pind Daan and Tarpan. 4) Invoking Lord Narayana for the liberation of the soul. 5) Immersing the effigy in a sacred river.

content.shloka: Nagbali is a companion ritual performed alongside Narayan Bali. It is done to atone for the sin of killing a serpent (Sarpa Hatya) — whether knowingly or unknowingly — by any ancestor, which causes Naga Dosha in the family.
content.meaning: Symptoms of Naga Dosha include skin diseases, obstacles in marriage, childlessness, and repeated snake sightings or dreams. The Nagbali ritual involves worshipping Naga Devata and performing specific offerings to pacify the serpent deities.
content.transliteration: Nagbali is a companion ritual performed alongside Narayan Bali. It is done to atone for the sin of killing a serpent (Sarpa Hatya) — whether knowingly or unknowingly — by any ancestor, which causes Naga Dosha in the family.

content.shloka:
Om Sarpa sarpa maha sarpa kshamasva mama dushkritam |
Tava kopa prashamanam Naag Bali prakaashitam ||
content.meaning: O Serpent, great Serpent, forgive my misdeeds. To calm your anger, this Nag Bali ritual is being performed. Both rituals together — Narayan Bali and Nagbali — provide complete liberation from ancestral afflictions.
content.transliteration:
Om Sarpa sarpa mahā sarpa kṣamasva mama duṣkṛtaṁ |
Tava kopa praśamanaṁ Nāga Bali prakāśitaṁ ||

content.shloka:
Om ye bandhavaa abandhavaa ye anya janmani baandhavaah |
Te sarve triptim aayaantu ye cha asmat udakam ichchhanti ||
content.meaning: May all those who are related to us, those who are not related, and those who were related in previous births — may they all be satisfied. And may all those who desire this water offering receive it.
content.transliteration:
Om ye bāndhavā abandhavā ye anya janmani bāndhavāḥ |
Te sarve tṛptim āyāntu ye cāsmat udakaṁ icchanti ||

content.shloka:
Om oorjam vahantee amritam ghritam payah kilaalam parisrutam svadhaa |
Tarpayata me pitrin ||
content.meaning: O waters carrying energy, nectar, ghee, milk, and juice — along with Svadha (the sacred offering), satisfy my ancestors.
content.transliteration:
Om ūrjaṁ vahantī amṛtaṁ ghṛtaṁ payaḥ kilālaṁ parisrutaṁ svadhā |
Tarpayata me pitṝn ||

content.shloka:
Om Madhu vaataa ritaayate Madhu ksharanti sindhavah |
Maadhveer nah santvaushadhih |
Madhu naktamutoshasee Madhu mat paarthivam rajah |
Madhu dyaurastu nah pitaa ||
content.meaning: May the winds blow sweetly for the righteous. May the rivers flow with honey. May the herbs be full of sweetness. May the nights and dawns be sweet. May the earth's dust be sweet. May the sky be a sweet father to us.
content.transliteration:
Om Madhu vātā ṛtāyate Madhu kṣaranti sindhavaḥ |
Mādhvīr naḥ santvoṣadhīḥ |
Madhu naktam utoṣasī Madhu mat pārthivaṁ rajaḥ |
Madhu dyaur astu naḥ pitā ||

content.shloka:
Om Pitarah pitaamahaa ye cha prapitaamahaa ye chaagne kavyavaahana |
Teebhir indra sajoshah svadhaam imam aadhaataa ||
content.meaning: O Agni, bearer of offerings to the ancestors — my fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers — along with Indra, may You accept this Svadha offering.
content.transliteration:
Om Pitaraḥ pitāmahā ye ca prapitāmahā ye cāgne kavyavāhana |
Tībhir Indra sajoṣāḥ svadhām imām ādhātā ||

content.shloka:
Closing Mantra:
Om dyauh shaantih antariksham shaantih prithivee shaantih
Aapah shaantih oshadhayah shaantih vanaspatayah shaantih |
Vishve devaah shaantih Brahma shaantih sarvam shaantih
Shaantireva shaantih saa maa shaantiredhi |
Om Shaantih Shaantih Shaantih ||
content.meaning: May there be peace in heaven, peace in the sky, peace on earth. May the waters, herbs, and trees be peaceful. May all the gods be at peace, may Brahman be at peace, may everything be at peace. May that peace, real peace, be mine. Om Peace, Peace, Peace.
content.transliteration:
Om dyauḥ śāntiḥ antarikṣaṁ śāntiḥ pṛthivī śāntiḥ
Āpaḥ śāntiḥ oṣadhayaḥ śāntiḥ vanaspatayaḥ śāntiḥ |
Viśve devāḥ śāntiḥ Brahma śāntiḥ sarvaṁ śāntiḥ
Śāntir eva śāntiḥ sā mā śāntir edhi |
Om Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ ||
